issues.legal_issue: A co-owner who collects rents from jointly owned property is not liable for pre-suit interest on another co-owner’s share merely because of that collection, absent a recognized basis for interest or a breach of trust.
material_facts: After dissolution of a partnership, the defendant possessed jointly owned properties and collected rents from them; the plaintiffs claimed half the rental income.
The agreements between the parties did not provide for interest, and no applicable substantive law otherwise made interest payable.
There was no allegation or finding that the defendant gained an advantage in derogation of the plaintiffs’ rights by using his position as co-owner.
There was no breach of trust or obligation to pay the plaintiffs’ share at fixed intervals or on demand.
issues.conclusion: The plaintiffs were not entitled to pre-suit interest on their share of the rental income. Interest was payable at six per cent per annum only from the date of the final decree on the amount found due.
issues.legal_principle: Pre-suit interest may be awarded where an agreement, a binding trade usage, or substantive law authorizes it. Section 1 of the Interest Act, 1839 does not independently authorize interest unless the circumstances attract equitable jurisdiction; it also provides for interest where a certain sum is payable at a certain time under a written instrument. Under sections 90 and 95 of the Trusts Act, 1882, a co-owner does not become a trustee merely by collecting all rents: the required advantage must be gained by availing oneself of the co-ownership position and in derogation of other interested persons’ rights. Under section 23, interest for breach of trust is confined to the stated circumstances; unreasonable delay under section 23(b) concerns an obligation to pay trust money at fixed intervals or on demand. The Court relied on Bengal Nagpur Railway Co. Ltd. v. Ruttanji Ramji, Thawardas Pherumal v. Union of India, Union of India v. Rallia Ram, Union of India v. Watkins Mayor & Co., Blogg v. Johnson, Silkstone and Haigh Moor Coal Co. v. Edey, Malland v. Gray, and Guildrey v. Stevens.

rule.if: partition_and_accounting_proceeding and co_owner_collected_joint_rents and no_agreement_for_interest and no_applicable_law_authorized_interest and no_fixed_sum_due_under_written_instrument and no_advantage_in_derogation_found and no_breach_of_trust and no_fixed_or_demand_payment_obligation

predicates.partition_and_accounting_proceeding: The proceeding sought division of jointly owned property and an account of income from it.
predicates.co_owner_collected_joint_rents: A co-owner in possession collected rents from jointly owned property.
predicates.no_agreement_for_interest: The parties had made no agreement requiring interest on the collected rents.
predicates.no_applicable_law_authorized_interest: No applicable substantive legal rule independently made interest payable on the claimed amount.
predicates.no_fixed_sum_due_under_written_instrumen: No written instrument made a certain sum payable at a certain time.
predicates.no_advantage_in_derogation_found: No advantage gained by using the co-ownership position to the detriment of other interested persons was alleged or found.
predicates.no_breach_of_trust: The court found no breach of trust by the person who collected the rents.
predicates.no_fixed_or_demand_payment_obligation: There was no obligation to pay the beneficiaries’ money at fixed intervals or on demand.

issues.definition: When a co-owner collects joint rents in a partition and accounting proceeding, the stated absence of an independent basis for interest, a detrimental advantage, a breach of trust, and a fixed or demand payment obligation results in pre-suit interest not being payable.

issues.legal_issue: An appellate court may determine a later-period share of income from the record rather than remand for further accounting where the record permits an estimate and the litigation has already been prolonged.
material_facts: The commissioner’s examination of the accounts covered an earlier period than the later period for which the plaintiffs were also awarded a share of rental income.
The High Court had treated the rental income shown for the earlier period as a basis for the later-period award, and the Supreme Court considered that assumption insufficiently supported.
The litigation had already continued for a prolonged period, and the Supreme Court chose not to remand the matter after examining the evidence on record.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court reduced the amount allowed for the later period, determining the plaintiffs’ share from the evidence on record instead of remanding for a further inquiry.
issues.legal_principle: The Court held that the later-period award lacked a sufficient basis in the commissioner’s account, but declined to remand because of the prolonged litigation and determined an appropriate amount from the evidence available. No statute or earlier case is cited for this determination.

rule.if: appeal_from_accounting_decree and later_period_income_not_established_by_examined_accounts and record_permits_estimation and litigation_prolonged

predicates.appeal_from_accounting_decree: The proceeding is an appeal from a decree determining income payable after an accounting.
predicates.later_period_income_not_established_by_e: The accounts examined did not establish the income for the later period in dispute.
predicates.record_permits_estimation: The evidence already on record permits the appellate court to estimate the amount due for that period.
predicates.litigation_prolonged: The case has already been litigated for a prolonged time.

issues.definition: If an accounting appeal concerns a later period not established by the examined accounts, but the record permits an estimate and the litigation is prolonged, the appellate court may estimate the income due without remanding.

issues.legal_issue: A limitation objection to an appeal cannot be entertained at a later appellate stage when it was not pressed below and the lower appellate court made no finding on it.
material_facts: The appellant argued that the plaintiffs’ appeal to the High Court was out of time.
The High Court judgment contained no finding on limitation, and the Supreme Court concluded that the objection had not been pressed when that appeal was heard.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court declined to entertain the limitation objection in the absence of a finding by the High Court.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the lack of a lower-court finding, in circumstances where the objection had not been pressed below, as preventing consideration of the objection at the present appellate stage. No statute or earlier case is cited for this determination.

predicates.appeal_from_lower_appellate_decision: The proceeding is a further appeal from a lower appellate decision.
predicates.limitation_objection_not_pressed_below: The party raising the limitation objection did not press it before the lower appellate court.
predicates.lower_appellate_court_made_no_limitation: The lower appellate court made no finding on whether the appeal was in time.

issues.definition: In a further appeal, an objection to limitation that was not pressed below and was not decided below is not entertained by the higher court.

issues.legal_issue: A claim of vacancies may be rejected in an accounting dispute where the person responsible for the rental accounts has not kept proper accounts, even though liability cannot be based simply on rent that was never realized from unlet premises.
material_facts: The defendant managed the properties and the High Court found that he had not kept proper accounts of the rent realized from the shops.
The defendant relied on vacancies to contest the rental-income calculation.

The Supreme Court observed that constructive-trustee liability could not be imposed merely for rent not realized from tenants or premises that were unlet, but upheld the High Court’s finding because of the inadequate accounts.
issues.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the challenge to the High Court’s treatment of vacancies, holding that its finding was not vitiated by an error of law because proper accounts had not been kept.
issues.legal_principle: A person cannot be held as a constructive trustee for rent that was not realized from tenants or for premises that were not let. However, where the person responsible for the rental accounts has not kept proper accounts, the court need not accept that person’s assertions about vacancies. The Court referred to sections 90 and 95 of the Trusts Act, 1882 in discussing constructive trusteeship.

predicates.appeal_from_rental_accounting_finding: The proceeding challenges a finding about rental income in an accounting dispute.
predicates.person_responsible_for_rent_accounts_kep: The person responsible for collecting or accounting for rents did not keep proper rental accounts.
predicates.vacancy_claim_not_supported_by_proper_ac: The claimed vacancies are not supported by proper rental accounts.

issues.definition: In an appeal concerning rental accounting, inadequate accounts kept by the person responsible for them may permit the court to reject an unsupported claim of vacancies.
